posts.title: Why Every Quiet Grid Press Puzzle Has One Solution
posts.summary: Open a Sudoku book to any page and you are trusting the maker of that book with one thing above all: that the puzzle in front of you has exactly one answer.
posts.body:
Open a Sudoku book to any page and you are trusting the maker of that book with one thing above all: that the puzzle in front of you has exactly one answer.

It sounds obvious. It is not automatic. A grid can look like a Sudoku, follow every rule of the game, and still have two or three ways to finish. You work for twenty minutes, reach a point where two numbers could both be right, and the puzzle quietly lets you down. Nothing on the page tells you that it was never your fault.

What we do about it

Every puzzle in a Quiet Grid Press book comes from our own puzzle library. Before a grid is allowed into a book, the library solves it and confirms that one solution, and only one, exists. A grid that fails that check is never printed. It is the quiet part of the work: nobody sees it, and the only sign of it is that every puzzle you finish simply makes sense.

The library also records which puzzles have gone into which book, so a grid you solved in one of our books will not turn up again in another.

What Easy means

The second thing a label promises is difficulty. In our books, an Easy puzzle is one that can be finished with plain logic: scanning a row, a column or a box, finding the square that can hold only one number, writing it in, and moving on. No guessing. If a puzzle needs a trick that almost nobody would find, it does not belong in an Easy book, however nice it looks on the page.

We print the label on every puzzle page, with the stars beside it, so that you know before you start what you are sitting down to.

What the answer pages show

At the back of every book, the solutions are printed six to a page. The numbers that were given to you at the start are lightly shaded, so you can see at a glance which squares were yours. Nothing else is highlighted, and there are no boxes inside boxes; it is the finished grid, as plainly as we can print it.

Where the checking happens

The checking happens before a book is built, not after it is printed. Each grid is kept in the puzzle library together with its solution and its record: which book it went into, how hard it is, and where it has been used. A grid that has already been printed in one of our books is recorded there, so the next book starts from a clean list. Every page is built from that record, so the puzzle you see is the puzzle that was checked.

Why it matters to us

A puzzle is recreation. Good recreation keeps its promises. We would rather print fewer puzzles and have every one of them be right than print more and leave a reader stuck on a grid that was never fair. If you have ever finished one of our puzzles and felt that small click as the last square fell into place, that is what the checking was for.

posts.title: A Verse with Every Puzzle: How the Psalms Book Is Arranged
posts.summary: Every puzzle in a Bible Verse Sudoku book has a verse beside it. In Book 2, Psalms, those 120 verses are not in the order the Bible prints them. They are arranged as a journey, and the journey is the one the Psalms themselves make: from praise to trust.
posts.body:
Every puzzle in a Bible Verse Sudoku book has a verse beside it. In Book 2, Psalms, those 120 verses are not in the order the Bible prints them. They are arranged as a journey, and the journey is the one the Psalms themselves make: from praise to trust.

Twelve chapters, ten puzzles each

The book opens with The Heavens Declare, where creation does the praising, and A Joyful Noise, where the people join in. His Mercy Endures gathers the Psalms that repeat that line until it stays with you.

Then the book turns honest. Honest Prayer holds the Psalms that ask how long, and why, and where are you. The Psalms do not skip that part, so neither does the book. The Blessed Way and Teach Us to Number Our Days bring the wisdom Psalms, and A Lamp unto My Feet the ones about the word itself.

The King's Strength and A Righteous Reign look to the king, and through him to the Lord who reigns. And then the last three chapters come to rest: The Lord Is My Shepherd, Refuge and Strength, and A Quiet Heart.

The final puzzle in the book, number 120, carries Psalms 23:6: Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life: and I will dwell in the house of the LORD for ever. That is where the Psalms arrive, and that is where the book ends.

Reading the book in order

The chapters follow the movement of the Psalms themselves, so a reader who works through from the first puzzle meets praise first and trust last. A reader who opens the book at random will still find each puzzle complete on its own page, with its verse and its drawing, and will not need the chapter before it.

How a verse is chosen

Each verse is printed exactly as the King James Version gives it, including the capitals in LORD where the Bible prints them, and cited by chapter and verse. We do not shorten a verse to fit. If a verse is long, the page makes room for it. Across the whole seven-book series, no verse appears in two books; each one was chosen for the chapter it sits in.

How the drawing is chosen

Every verse has a small pencil drawing of its own, placed at the foot of the puzzle. The drawing answers the verse rather than decorating it: a lamp for a lamp, still water for still water. In the Psalms book the drawings stay close to the world the Psalms were sung in, and each one carries a sign of light and a sign of being kept.

How the puzzle is chosen

The puzzles are all Easy. Each one was made and checked in our own puzzle library to have exactly one solution, and each can be finished by scanning rows, columns and boxes for the square that can hold only one number. The verse sets the tone; the puzzle gives you the quiet half hour to sit with it.

The answer pages carry verses too, so that even the checking is a small reading.

Bible Verse Sudoku: Psalms is Book 2 of seven. If the Psalms are the part of the Bible you return to, this is the book we made for you.

posts.title: The Habit That Solves More Sudoku Than Any Trick
posts.summary: There are many named techniques for Sudoku, and most of them are worth learning eventually. But one plain habit finishes more Easy puzzles than all of them together, and it takes about a minute to learn.
posts.body:
There are many named techniques for Sudoku, and most of them are worth learning eventually. But one plain habit finishes more Easy puzzles than all of them together, and it takes about a minute to learn.

The habit

  1. Pick a row, a column, or a 3 by 3 box. Any one will do; start with the one that has the most numbers already filled in.
  2. Find a number that is missing from it. Ask: which empty square in this row, column or box can hold that number? Look along the lines that cross each empty square. If a number already appears in the row and column that meet at a square, that square cannot hold it.
  3. When only one square is left that can hold the number, write it in. Then move on to the next missing number, or the next row, column or box.

That is the whole habit. Scan, ask, check, write, move on.

Why it works

Every Easy puzzle in a Quiet Grid Press book can be finished with this habit alone, because that is how we define Easy: no guessing, no advanced trick, just the square that can hold only one number, found again and again until the grid is full. If you reach a point where nothing seems to move, you have not failed; you have simply not found the next one yet. Go back to the row, column or box with the most numbers in it, and start the scan again.

Three small helps

Use a pencil. Not because you will be wrong often, but because a pencil keeps the page calm. A soft eraser is part of the kit.

Count to nine. When a row or box has six or seven numbers in it, say the missing ones out loud, or write them lightly in the margin. Our pages leave room in the margins for exactly this.

Slow down when it gets easy. The last ten squares of a grid go quickly, and that is where most mistakes happen. Check each number against its row, its column and its box before you write it.

Where a habit goes wrong

The most common mistake is writing a number too early. A square looks as if it can hold a number, because nothing in its own row or column stops it, but the box it sits in already holds that number somewhere else. Scan the box as well as the row and the column. The second most common mistake is the rush at the end, covered above. Both are fixed by the same habit: slow down a little, look at all three lines through the square, and then write.

What this habit is not

It is not a race. There is no timer on our pages and no score at the back. The point of a quiet half hour with a grid is the half hour, and the small click when the last square falls into place. Slow and steady finishes more grids than fast and frantic.

Try it on the next Easy puzzle you open. If you notice something along the way, we would be glad to hear it.

posts.title: Seven Books, One Series: Bible Verse Sudoku
posts.summary: When we made Bible Verse Sudoku, we had one book in mind: 120 Easy puzzles, a verse from the King James Version beside each one, and enough white space that the page felt like a place to sit down. We did not plan a series. The series came from the verses.
posts.body:
When we made Bible Verse Sudoku, we had one book in mind: 120 Easy puzzles, a verse from the King James Version beside each one, and enough white space that the page felt like a place to sit down. We did not plan a series. The series came from the verses.

A hundred and twenty verses is a small number. The Psalms alone could fill a book, and the sayings of Jesus another, and the women of the Bible a third. So Bible Verse Sudoku became Book 1 of seven, and the other six each take one theme and give it the room it deserves.

The seven themes

Bible Verse Sudoku (Book 1) moves through twelve chapters from light and creation to the steady journey home: trust, wisdom, courage, peace, love, hope, gratitude, service, mercy and fellowship along the way.

Psalms (Book 2) follows the Psalms from praise to trust. It begins with the heavens declaring and a joyful noise, makes room for honest prayer, walks the blessed way, and comes to rest with the Lord as shepherd, refuge and keeper of a quiet heart.

Proverbs and Ecclesiastes (Book 3) walks from the beginning of wisdom to the whole duty: counsel, words, diligent hands, honest dealing, patience, friends and neighbors, home, humility, and a time for everything from Ecclesiastes.

The Words of Jesus (Book 4) holds 120 sayings from Matthew, Mark, Luke and John in the order the Gospels tell them, from the call by the Sea of Galilee to the promise, lo, I am with you alway.

Parables (Book 5) goes from the field to the table: the sower, the mustard seed, the pearl, the lost sheep, the prodigal son, the good Samaritan, the talents, the two builders, the ten virgins and the great supper.

Women of Scripture (Book 6) moves from faith to witness: Sarah, Miriam, Hannah, Deborah, Esther, Ruth, Mary, and the women who came to the tomb.

Journeys (Book 7) sets out with Abram and comes home: the Exodus, the wilderness, the Jordan, exile and return, the roads to Emmaus and Damascus, the voyages of Paul, and the pilgrims who seek a better country.

What is the same in every book

Every book has 120 Easy puzzles in twelve chapters of ten. Every puzzle has its own page, with the verse printed exactly as the King James Version gives it, cited by book, chapter and verse, and a small pencil drawing that answers that verse. Every puzzle has been checked to have exactly one solution. Complete solutions are at the back, six to a page. The books are 8.5 by 11 inches, 158 pages, black and white.

Easy means what it says. Each puzzle can be finished with plain logic, scanning rows, columns and boxes for the square that can hold only one number. There is no guessing, and there is no score to keep.

Where to find them

Book 1 is on Amazon now. The other six are arriving one at a time, and our books page shows which are available today. If one of the seven themes is yours, or belongs to someone you know, we hope it finds its way to a quiet table and a sharp pencil.
